persona: Apparel art director for independent labels

designs.title: Vitis vinifera
designs.why: The most retail-ready of the three. It has real engraving-plate line quality: the stipple shading on the grapes and the serrated leaf edges hold up crisp at full size, and the single-ink line weight sits nicely on a white tee without a heavy ink block. The italic Latin name with the plain-English caption in parentheses reads like a proper herbarium plate, which a wine or natural-history buyer will pay $50 for. Its weak spot is the layout: the pruned cane floats off to the right as a separate island, and the left caption hangs in empty space, so from 3 m the piece reads as a branch plus an afterthought.
designs.fix: Bring the pruned cane into the main group: move it closer and align its top and its caption baseline with the branch, so the whole plate reads as one block with a deliberate border of white space.

designs.title: Fermentation
designs.why: A strong idea for brewers, and the inverted white-on-black version leads well: the cutaway tank, the CO2 bubble field and the magnified yeast inset make a clear patent-diagram shape, and the serif labels are readable at full size. On the back, though, the print sits as a tall, thin column, and at a glance the dense bubble field turns into grey noise. The yeast inset also has drafting slips. The 'Budding yeast cell' leader forks, and one branch points at a stray speck. There are loose specks and ticks around the circle that look like scan dirt rather than intent.
designs.fix: Clean up the yeast inset: give each label one leader that lands on its target, and delete the stray specks and ticks. Then thin the bubble field slightly so the tank interior reads as texture rather than grey when the shirt is seen from a few metres away.

designs.title: Shaping
designs.why: The subject is right for a surf label, but the execution looks auto-traced rather than drawn. Up close the line breaks into broken dashes and gritty clumps: the board's outline is a dotted, interrupted edge, the hands and planer go mushy, and the stools and dust are fuzzy blobs. At about 27% ink coverage it is a heavy, uneven block on the tee. The generic spaced sans 'SHAPING' over a hairline rule feels like a default placeholder, not a label mark.
designs.fix: Redraw it as clean, controlled linework: a solid board outline, deliberate hatching instead of gritty texture, and a clear read of the hands and planer. Then replace the stock heading with typography that has character and belongs to the illustration's era.
